segments.voice: Last week, the Gayatri and the peace chants took the verse apart down to dhiyo yo nah: who, our thoughts, and the who is the god. One word left.

Nani tells it at the table, chai going cold. A girl in a small flat, years ago. Every morning, through the thin wall, her father's voice at the same hour, low and even, the same three lines. She learns them the way you learn a song from the next room: sound first, every syllable, no meaning at all. Years go by like that. Then one morning, grown, with her own kettle on, she finally asks someone what the last word means. Priya leans in. Nani says: it means push.
screen: `A VOICE THROUGH A THIN WALL.` → `SOUND FIRST. MEANING LATER.`

segments.voice: The last word is prachodayat. Pra- means forward, onward. The rest comes from a verb meaning to urge, to set in motion. Together: urge forward, spur on, push. The ending marks he, someone other than the speakers, and the form is a wish: not he does, but may he. So the sentence finishes. Who? The god, Savitr. What? Our thoughts. Doing what? May he stir them forward. Here's the detail worth telling someone: it's the only word in the verse that moves something else. Everything before it is held, described, turned toward. Then one verb pushes. And it fits. Savitr is the god who sets things going; the last verb asks him to do exactly that, with minds. Now the whole verse, rebuilt: tat savitur varenyam, bhargo devasya dhimahi, dhiyo yo nah prachodayat. We hold in mind that worth-choosing radiance of the god Savitr; may he stir our thoughts. Two verbs. A pointing word, a whose, a choice, a shining, a we, and a push. Nani's story ends there. Priya says she'll keep the Gayatri for home, the way her dad asked, and find a peace chant for the stage.
screen: `PRA-: FORWARD. URGE ON.` · `MAY HE: A WISH.` · `THE ONLY WORD THAT MOVES ANYTHING.` · `THE WHOLE VERSE, REBUILT.` · then, large: `MAY HE STIR OUR THOUGHTS.`

segments.voice: Close your eyes and notice the very start of each in-breath, the small push that begins it without your deciding. Rest in that beginning, again and again. If the Gayatri is part of your practice, you can say it once, silently, at the end; if not, hold its English: may our thoughts be stirred.
The Gayatri and the peace chants. Today's piece: prachodayat, may he stir, the last verb, and the Gayatri read whole.

notes: Last Gayatri word day (1499–1506). Grammar stated: pra- 'forward'; the verb from cud 'urge, impel' in a causative form; third person singular; read as a wish. Roots and tense labels kept out of the voice. Confirm.
